title: The Gut in the Body Cavities
subject: Gastrointestinal System (GAST)
author: Dr. Sharilyn Rennie

overview.intro: This chapter places the gut within the body cavities: the course of the esophagus through the neck and mediastinum, the nerve supply of the tongue, the peritoneal sacs and the ligaments that carry vessels to the upper abdominal organs, the inguinal region where hernias form, and the dependent spaces where fluid collects. Board questions here usually give a finding, such as a lodged pill, a deviated tongue, a groin bulge, or fluid on ultrasound, and ask which structure or space is involved. Most of this anatomy follows from development: rotation of the stomach, the pharyngeal arch origins of the tongue, and descent of the gonads explain the relations you need to remember.

connections.how: Gastric rotation creates the lesser sac and turns the vagal trunks, and the liver and spleen take their ligaments from the ventral and dorsal mesenteries.

connections.to: Gut blood supply and portal circulation (GI-5)
connections.how: The lower esophagus, the falciform ligament, and the short gastric veins are sites where portal and systemic veins connect and enlarge in portal hypertension.
Zenker diverticulum and dysphagia from extrinsic compression arise at the narrowings and relations described for the esophagus.
Ascites, peritonitis, and abscesses spread along the gutters and pool in the dependent recesses described here.
Lesions of CN V3, VII, IX, X, and XII each leave a distinct pattern of tongue sensation, taste, and movement.

terms.def: The part of the thoracic midline space behind the pericardium, containing the esophagus, descending aorta, azygos veins, and thoracic duct.
The cricopharyngeal part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor, a band of skeletal muscle that keeps the top of the esophagus closed between swallows.
A branch of the facial nerve that carries taste from the anterior two thirds of the tongue and parasympathetic fibers to the submandibular ganglion.
A double fold of peritoneum connecting an organ to another organ or to the abdominal wall, carrying vessels and nerves between its layers.
The part of the peritoneal cavity behind the stomach and lesser omentum, opening into the greater sac only through the omental foramen.
The opening between the lesser and greater sacs, bounded in front by the hepatoduodenal ligament and behind by the inferior vena cava.
The hepatic portal vein, proper hepatic artery, and common bile duct, carried together in the hepatoduodenal ligament.
A fetal pouch of peritoneum that precedes the testis through the abdominal wall and normally closes after descent.
The area of the lower anterior abdominal wall bounded by the inferior epigastric vessels, the lateral edge of rectus abdominis, and the inguinal ligament.
A peritoneal channel lateral to the ascending or descending colon that connects the upper abdomen with the pelvis.
The lowest part of a body cavity for a given posture, where free fluid collects under gravity.

sections.title: Course and narrowings of the esophagus

blocks.text: The esophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long that carries a bolus from the pharynx to the stomach. It begins at the lower border of the cricoid cartilage, level with C6, where the cricopharyngeal part of the inferior pharyngeal constrictor forms the upper esophageal sphincter. Its muscle changes from skeletal in roughly the upper third to smooth in the lower third, so diseases of skeletal muscle disturb the start of swallowing while loss of myenteric neurons disturbs the lower esophagus.

In the neck the esophagus lies behind the trachea and in front of the vertebral column, slightly to the left. It enters the superior mediastinum through the thoracic inlet, still between the trachea and the vertebrae, and then descends in the posterior mediastinum behind the left main bronchus, the pericardium, and the left atrium. The descending aorta lies at first to its left and then behind it, as the esophagus moves forward and to the left to reach the esophageal hiatus, formed by fibers of the right crus of the diaphragm at T10. A short abdominal segment joins the cardia of the stomach at about T11.

blocks.text: At each narrowing a muscle ring or a firm neighboring structure keeps the lumen from widening, so a slowly moving bolus, coin, or tablet tends to stop there. A tablet held against the mucosa dissolves in place and releases a concentrated irritant solution that ulcerates the wall (pill esophagitis), classically at the aortic arch when a pill is taken with little water at bedtime. The same relations explain extrinsic compression: an enlarged left atrium, as in mitral stenosis, indents the anterior wall of the middle esophagus on a barium swallow and can cause dysphagia, as can an aortic aneurysm or enlarged subcarinal lymph nodes.

Just above the cricopharyngeus, the posterior pharyngeal wall has a weak area between the thyropharyngeal and cricopharyngeal parts of the inferior constrictor (Killian triangle). When the cricopharyngeus does not relax fully, swallowing pressure pushes mucosa and submucosa out through this gap as a Zenker diverticulum, a false diverticulum that traps food and causes regurgitation and halitosis. At the lower end, a sudden pressure rise against a closed sphincter during forceful vomiting can tear the full wall (Boerhaave syndrome), usually on the left posterolateral side just above the diaphragm.

The two vagus nerves form the esophageal plexus on the lower esophagus and leave it as two trunks through the hiatus. Because the stomach rotates during development, the left vagus becomes the anterior trunk and the right vagus the posterior trunk. The lower esophagus is also a portosystemic junction: esophageal tributaries of the left gastric vein (portal) connect with veins draining to the azygos system (systemic), so portal hypertension dilates these submucosal veins into varices (GI-5).

blocks.predict: A 70-year-old with mitral stenosis has difficulty swallowing solid food. Where would a barium swallow show the esophagus indented, and why there?
blocks.explain: On the anterior wall of the middle thoracic esophagus, below the aortic and bronchial impressions, because the left atrium (in the middle mediastinum) lies directly in front of the esophagus, which descends in the posterior mediastinum.

sections.title: Innervation of the tongue and lesion patterns

blocks.text: The nerve supply of the tongue follows its embryology. The mucosa of the anterior two thirds develops from the first pharyngeal arch, so its general sensation (touch, pain, and temperature) is carried by the nerve of that arch, the mandibular division of the trigeminal nerve (CN V3), through its lingual branch. The posterior third develops mainly from the third arch, so the glossopharyngeal nerve (CN IX) carries both general sensation and taste there, including the vallate papillae just in front of the V-shaped sulcus terminalis. A small area at the root near the epiglottis, from the fourth arch, is supplied by the vagus (CN X) through the internal laryngeal nerve.

Taste from the anterior two thirds does not travel centrally with V3. It is carried by the chorda tympani, a branch of the facial nerve (CN VII) that leaves the facial canal, crosses the middle ear, and joins the lingual nerve in the infratemporal fossa. Its taste fibers have their cell bodies in the geniculate ganglion and end, like the taste fibers of CN IX and CN X, in the nucleus of the solitary tract. The chorda tympani also carries preganglionic parasympathetic fibers, which leave the lingual nerve to synapse in the submandibular ganglion that supplies the submandibular and sublingual glands.

The tongue muscles develop from occipital somites and bring their own nerve, the hypoglossal nerve (CN XII), which supplies all intrinsic muscles and the extrinsic genioglossus, hyoglossus, and styloglossus. The exception is palatoglossus, which develops with the muscles of the soft palate and is supplied by the vagus through the pharyngeal plexus. Each genioglossus pulls the tongue forward and toward the opposite side, so when both contract equally the tongue protrudes in the midline.

blocks.caption: Deficits are on the side of the lesion. Sensation and taste of the anterior two thirds travel in different nerves; the posterior third uses CN IX for both.

blocks.text: Two motor patterns are tested most. In a lower motor neuron lesion of CN XII, the genioglossus on the injured side is paralyzed, so the healthy muscle pushes the protruded tongue toward the weak side, and denervation produces atrophy and fasciculations on that side. In an upper motor neuron lesion, such as a cortical stroke, corticobulbar input to genioglossus is mainly crossed, so the tongue deviates away from the side of the brain lesion, without atrophy.

blocks.title: Localizing a lesion from the tongue examination
blocks.text: After removal of a lower right third molar, a patient has lost touch and taste on the right anterior two thirds of the tongue, with normal posterior third sensation, gag reflex, and protrusion. Touch loss localizes to the lingual nerve; taste loss as well places the injury beyond the point where the chorda tympani joins it, which fits the lingual nerve lying against the inner mandible beside the third molar. A facial nerve lesion in the facial canal above the chorda tympani instead removes taste but keeps touch, with facial weakness. A lesion at the stylomastoid foramen spares taste, because the chorda tympani has already left.

sections.title: Greater and lesser sacs, omenta, and the omental foramen

blocks.text: Parietal peritoneum lines the abdominal wall and visceral peritoneum covers the organs, with the peritoneal cavity, a potential space holding a thin film of fluid, between them. Double folds connecting an organ to the wall or to another organ are called mesenteries, ligaments, or omenta, and they carry the organ's vessels, nerves, and lymphatics. The cavity has a large greater sac and a small lesser sac (omental bursa).

The lesser sac is a product of gastric rotation. The stomach originally hangs between a dorsal mesogastrium and a ventral mesogastrium. As it rotates about 90 degrees clockwise around its long axis (viewed from above), its left side comes to face forward and the dorsal mesogastrium is swept to the left, opening a recess behind the stomach. The liver grows into the ventral mesogastrium, which becomes the falciform ligament in front of the liver and the lesser omentum between the liver and the stomach. The dorsal mesogastrium elongates into the greater omentum.

blocks.caption: The same rotation brings the left vagus to the front of the stomach.

blocks.text: The lesser omentum runs from the lesser curvature and the first 2 cm of the duodenum to the liver. Its larger part, the hepatogastric ligament, attaches to the fissure for the ligamentum venosum, and its thick right free edge, the hepatoduodenal ligament, runs to the porta hepatis. The greater omentum hangs like an apron from the greater curvature, folds back on itself, and attaches to the transverse colon; its layers usually fuse, so the lesser sac extends only a short way into it. The omentum is mobile and adheres to inflamed organs, which helps wall off local infection.

blocks.caption: The omental foramen is the only natural communication between the sacs.

blocks.text: The hepatoduodenal ligament carries the portal triad: the common bile duct in front on the right, the proper hepatic artery in front on the left, and the hepatic portal vein behind both. Because the ligament forms the front wall of the omental foramen and the inferior vena cava its back wall, compressing the free edge (Pringle maneuver) stops hepatic arterial and portal inflow to the liver, while bleeding from the hepatic veins or vena cava, which lie outside the ligament, continues.

These relations decide where fluid goes when the stomach is breached. A perforated ulcer on the posterior wall of the stomach releases its contents into the lesser sac, where they may stay contained or escape through the omental foramen into the right subhepatic space, whereas an anterior perforation spills directly into the greater sac and releases free air under the diaphragm. Fluid from acute pancreatitis also gathers in the lesser sac, because the pancreas forms its posterior wall, and a pseudocyst there can push the stomach forward.

blocks.predict: An ulcer perforates through the posterior wall of the stomach. Why may early signs of spreading peritonitis be limited, and where can the fluid leave the space it first enters?
blocks.explain: Gastric contents enter the lesser sac, which is closed except at the omental foramen, so fluid can only escape to the right through the foramen into the right subhepatic space and hepatorenal recess.

sections.title: Peritoneal ligaments and the vessels they carry

blocks.text: Each peritoneal ligament carries vessels between its two layers, so knowing its contents predicts which artery an ulcer erodes, which veins enlarge in portal hypertension, and which structure is at risk when an organ is freed. The ventral mesentery gives rise to the falciform ligament and the lesser omentum, which reach the liver. The dorsal mesogastrium gives rise to the gastrosplenic, splenorenal, and gastrocolic ligaments, which reach the greater curvature, the spleen, and the transverse colon.

blocks.text: The falciform ligament attaches the liver to the anterior abdominal wall and diaphragm and marks the surface boundary between the anatomical right and left lobes. Its free lower edge contains the ligamentum teres hepatis, the fibrous remnant of the left umbilical vein, which carried oxygenated placental blood to the fetal liver and closes after birth. Small paraumbilical veins run beside it, linking the left branch of the portal vein with veins of the abdominal wall around the umbilicus. When portal pressure rises, these portosystemic channels enlarge and radiate from the umbilicus as caput medusae (GI-5).

The gastrohepatic ligament carries the left gastric artery, a branch of the celiac trunk, and the right gastric artery, usually from the proper hepatic artery, which join along the lesser curvature, with companion veins that drain into the portal system. The left gastric vein also receives esophageal tributaries, so it is the main portal source of esophageal varices. A penetrating ulcer on the lesser curvature can erode the left gastric artery, whereas an ulcer in the posterior wall of the duodenal bulb erodes the gastroduodenal artery, which runs behind the duodenum outside these ligaments.

The spleen develops within the dorsal mesogastrium, so it stays tied to the stomach by the gastrosplenic ligament and to the posterior wall by the splenorenal ligament. The gastrosplenic ligament carries the short gastric vessels to the fundus and the left gastroepiploic vessels to the greater curvature. The splenorenal ligament carries the splenic artery and vein to the hilum together with the tail of the pancreas, the one part of the pancreas that is not retroperitoneal. Because the splenic vein runs directly behind the body and tail of the pancreas, pancreatitis or pancreatic cancer can cause it to thrombose, and splenic blood must then return through the short gastric veins.

sections.title: Inguinal canal, Hesselbach triangle, and groin hernias

blocks.text: The inguinal canal is an oblique passage about 4 cm long running inferomedially just above the medial half of the inguinal ligament. It carries the spermatic cord in males or the round ligament of the uterus in females, plus the ilioinguinal nerve, which enters partway along rather than through the deep ring. The canal exists because the testis, preceded by the processus vaginalis, descended through the wall and took a covering from each layer: external spermatic fascia (external oblique), cremaster (internal oblique), and internal spermatic fascia (transversalis fascia).

The deep (internal) ring is an opening in the transversalis fascia just above the midpoint of the inguinal ligament, lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels. The superficial (external) ring is a split in the external oblique aponeurosis just above and lateral to the pubic tubercle. Because the rings are offset, each weak point is backed by a strong wall, and straining contracts the arching roof muscles to flatten the canal like a valve.

blocks.text: Viewed from inside, the inferior epigastric vessels raise the lateral umbilical fold. The inguinal (Hesselbach) triangle lies medial to them, bounded laterally by these vessels, medially by the lateral edge of rectus abdominis, and inferiorly by the inguinal ligament. The fossa lateral to the fold leads to the deep ring.

Each hernia type follows a weak point. An indirect hernia follows the congenital route of testicular descent: it enters the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels through a processus vaginalis that did not close, travels inside all three cord coverings, and can reach the scrotum or labium majus. A direct hernia is acquired: transversalis fascia in the Hesselbach triangle weakens with age and repeated straining, and viscera bulge straight through medial to the vessels, outside the inner cord coverings. A femoral hernia passes below the inguinal ligament through the femoral ring, medial to the femoral vein. That ring is small and bounded by unyielding structures (inguinal ligament in front, pectineal ligament behind, lacunar ligament medially, femoral vein laterally), so femoral hernias are the most likely to incarcerate and strangulate.

blocks.title: Naming a hernia from its landmarks
blocks.text: A 68-year-old man with a chronic cough has a groin bulge above the inguinal ligament and medial to the pubic tubercle that does not enter the scrotum; from inside the abdomen, the defect lies medial to the lateral umbilical fold. Above the ligament and medial to the tubercle means inguinal, not femoral. The lateral umbilical fold is raised by the inferior epigastric vessels, so a defect medial to it lies in the Hesselbach triangle: a direct hernia, fitting chronic coughing against fascia weakened by age. A defect lateral to the fold would be at the deep ring, an indirect hernia.

sections.title: Dependent peritoneal spaces and abscess formation

blocks.text: Free fluid in the peritoneal cavity, whether ascites, blood, pus, or bile, follows the peritoneal attachments and gravity and collects in the lowest recess for the patient's position. The transverse mesocolon divides the cavity into supracolic and infracolic compartments, and the root of the small bowel mesentery divides the infracolic compartment into right and left spaces. The paracolic gutters, lateral to the ascending and descending colon, connect the upper abdomen with the pelvis.

In the supracolic compartment, the falciform ligament separates right and left subphrenic spaces between the diaphragm and the liver. Below the right lobe lies the right subhepatic space, whose posterior extension between the liver and right kidney is the hepatorenal recess (Morison pouch). When the patient is supine it is the most dependent part of the upper abdomen, and it opens into the right subphrenic space above, the right paracolic gutter below, and the lesser sac through the omental foramen. On the left, the phrenicocolic ligament, from the splenic flexure to the diaphragm, partly closes the top of the left gutter, so fluid moves less freely between the left upper quadrant and the pelvis.

When the patient is upright, the lowest part of the cavity is in the pelvis: the rectouterine pouch (of Douglas) between rectum and uterus, and the rectovesical pouch between rectum and bladder in men. Blood from a ruptured ectopic pregnancy and pus from appendicitis, diverticulitis, or pelvic inflammatory disease gather here. The rectouterine pouch lies just behind the posterior vaginal fornix and the rectovesical pouch in front of the rectum, so a pelvic collection can be felt on vaginal or rectal examination.

blocks.text: Fluid does not only fall. Each breath lowers pressure beneath the diaphragm, and lymphatic openings in the diaphragmatic peritoneum absorb fluid, so peritoneal fluid is drawn upward toward the subphrenic spaces, mainly along the open right paracolic gutter. This is why subphrenic abscesses follow perforated ulcers, appendicitis, and abdominal surgery, why they are more common on the right, and why pelvic infection can reach the liver capsule (perihepatitis in Fitz-Hugh-Curtis syndrome). The central diaphragmatic peritoneum is supplied by the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5), so its irritation is referred to the shoulder tip, whose skin is supplied by the supraclavicular nerves (C3, C4); the peripheral diaphragm is supplied by lower intercostal nerves, so irritation there is felt over the lower chest and upper abdominal wall.

integration.text: Embryology explains nearly every relation in this chapter. Rotation of the stomach creates the lesser sac and turns the vagal trunks, the liver growing into the ventral mesentery gives the falciform ligament and the route of the portal triad, the spleen forming in the dorsal mesogastrium gives its ligaments and its tie to the pancreatic tail, the arch origins of the tongue explain its split sensory supply, and descent of the testis explains the inguinal canal and the indirect hernia. When an anatomical rule seems arbitrary, its developmental origin usually makes sense of it.

The same anatomy routes disease. Portal hypertension opens collaterals in the lower esophagus, the falciform ligament, and the short gastric veins; perforation and pancreatitis fill the lesser sac; and infections from the appendix, colon, or fallopian tubes, whether mixed gut flora or Neisseria gonorrhoeae and Chlamydia trachomatis, collect in the dependent spaces. The limits are real: vessel origins, the extent of the lesser sac, and fusion of the omental layers vary between people, and fluid distribution also depends on volume, adhesions, and how long the patient has been in one position, so imaging findings are read together with the clinical picture.

summary: The esophagus runs from C6 behind the trachea and left atrium to the hiatus at T10, with narrowings at the cricopharyngeus, the aortic arch and left main bronchus, and the diaphragm.
Swallowed objects and tablets stall at the narrowings; an enlarged left atrium indents the middle esophagus from the front.
Anterior two thirds of the tongue: touch by the lingual nerve (V3), taste by the chorda tympani (VII); posterior third: touch and taste by CN IX.
CN XII moves the tongue except palatoglossus (CN X); a lower motor neuron CN XII lesion makes the tongue deviate toward the lesion.
Gastric rotation forms the lesser sac behind the stomach, which opens to the greater sac only through the omental foramen.
The hepatoduodenal ligament forms the front of the omental foramen and carries the bile duct (front right), hepatic artery (front left), and portal vein (behind); the IVC lies behind the foramen.
Falciform carries the ligamentum teres, gastrohepatic the gastric arteries, gastrosplenic the short gastric vessels, and splenorenal the splenic vessels and pancreatic tail.

Indirect hernias enter the deep ring lateral to the inferior epigastric vessels; direct hernias cross the Hesselbach triangle medial to them; femoral hernias pass below the inguinal ligament and strangulate most often.
Fluid pools in the hepatorenal recess when supine and in the rectouterine or rectovesical pouch when upright, and breathing draws it up the right gutter to the subphrenic spaces.
Subphrenic irritation of the central diaphragm is referred to the shoulder tip through the phrenic nerve (C3 to C5).
